properties.Session: TS: How well do we enable people to live fully until they die?
properties.Chairs: None Guillaume Economos, Dr María Avilés

content:
Research into Rehabilitation in Palliative Care.

1) What we mean by 'Living fully until you die' and why it matters is appraised through diverse lenses from person to population:
- ‘What matters most’: a research synthesis on priorities of people living with palliative diagnoses - invites audience reflection
- ‘The disability pandemic’: an interrogation of the impact of cancer, advanced chronic illness, multimorbidity, ageing and frailty on function, independence, care needs and costs - sets the context for rehabilitation as a solution.
2) Cutting-edge research and practice examples from high, middle and low-income countries illustrate the value of rehabilitation in palliative care and how to integrate it to enable people to live fully until they die:
- ‘Rehabilitation is everybody’s business’: towards a consensus definition and shared understanding- ‘From contradiction to evidence-based best practice’: history and literature- ‘A radical culture shift’ an integrated rehabilitative, palliative and geriatric approach for older people living with frailty.

Aim and learning objectives:

To challenge participants to consider how well they enable people with advanced, serious illness, old age or frailty to live fully until they die – critically interrogating what we mean by this founding aspiration of palliative care and how it is realised and evaluated in practice and research.
To expand participants' understanding of rehabilitation in palliative care as an integrated approach to enable people to live fully until they die through a compelling synthesis of research, innovative examples, international recommendations and an interactive expert panel discussion.

properties.Session: EAPC groups: Maximising the inclusivity of the public health approach to bereavement
properties.Chairs: Dr Steve Marshall, Prof Audrey Roulston, Ms Orla Keegan

content:
This session focuses on the research-based public health model for bereavement care. It poses questions for discussion on the translation of bereavement research into policy and practice, and more specifically, on implications for bereavement care for minoritised communities, including cultural and faith-based communities, those in prisons, the LGBTQI community, and people who are homeless. 
Session one is an initial overview of the public health model for bereavement care, compassionate communities and associated evidence. Session two is a data-driven case study on how the public health model is implemented in a large urban hospital setting, and session three outlines policy and practice implementation examples on how bereavement care is managed and rolled out through a range of marginalised settings. 
Three EAPC taskforces/reference groups will be represented: the Bereavement Taskforce, the Social Work Taskforce and the EAPC Public Health and Palliative Care Reference Group. 
Session aim: 
To explore a critical approach to the implementation of the public health bereavement model: integrating bereavement knowledge into practice for the benefit of all communities.  
Learning objectives:
• Integrate bereavement approaches across relevant task forces and reference groups at EAPC, including the Bereavement Taskforce, the Social Work Taskforce and the EAPC Public Health and Palliative Care Reference Group. 
• Identify the evidence base for an inclusive public health approach to bereavement care  
• Appraise the challenges and opportunities for translating bereavement research evidence into practice for all communities, including seldom heard and minority groups

Speakers:

Prof Samar Aoun, Perron Institute Research Chair in Palliative Care, The University of Western Australia.     EAPC Public Health and Palliative Care Reference Group. PRE-REC
Dr Steve Marshall, King’s College Hospital and King’s College London EAPC Social Work Taskforce 
Prof Audrey Roulston, Queen's University Belfast, Co-Chair EAPC Social Work Taskforce 
Irene Murphy and Orla Keegan, Co-Chairs EAPC Bereavement Taskforce

TS: Towards gold-standard methods in paediatric palliative care research, sharing knowledge, assessing challenges and opportunities.
properties.Chairs: Dr Martin Loučka, Dr María Avilés

content:
Research into Paediatric Palliative Care.

Effective delivery and adequate resourcing of healthcare rely on high-quality evidence to drive decisions. To date, PPC research has largely comprised small cohort studies (case studies, chart reviews, etc.).
Session aim:Explore opportunities and challenges in applying best-practice research methods to PPC research, through knowledge sharing across multiple disciplines, thereby strengthening the evidence base on which PPC delivery, resourcing, and planning decisions are made.

Learning objectives:Developing understanding and awareness of:-	opportunities for engaging with children and families in research-	real/perceived challenges in applying robust evaluation techniques in PPC (e.g., randomised controlled trials)-	methods for population-level planning of PPC.
The session will comprise three short presentations followed by structured discussion time.
Presentation 1 will focus on the increasingly vital role of Patient and Public Involvement (PPI) in health services research, specifically highlighting the engagement of children and young people (CYP). Prof Veronica Lambert will chart the evidence on CYP involvement as active PPI contributors across all stages of the PPC research cycle. 
Presentation 2 will examine real/perceived challenges to conducting randomised controlled trials and other robust evaluation techniques in PPC research. Prof Lorna Fraser will demonstrate the availability of core building blocks required for measuring effectiveness and cost effectiveness in PPC and discuss challenges and opportunities for advancing methods further.
Presentation 3 will highlight recent learnings from national level analysis on planning for PPC. Dr Samantha Smith will discuss challenges in defining need for PPC at a population-level, incorporating markers of complexity and applicability of methods to different data sources.

content:
Panel 1: Recruitment, equity and inclusion in trials
This panel will explore how equity, inclusion and diversity can be embedded across study design, consortium governance, implementation and dissemination, with attention to structural inequities in access, inclusive recruitment, culturally and linguistically appropriate methods, and equitable partnership models. The session will highlight practical strategies and measurable indicators.
Panellists: Lise Nottleman (INSPIRE), Everlien de Graaf (RAPHAEL), Nicola Cornally (In Touch) 

Panel 2: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence in palliative care research 
This panel will examine how AI can be responsibly integrated into research projects to enhance communication training, personalise care planning, support clinical decision-making, and generate real-world evidence, while addressing risks such as algorithmic bias, data governance, and digital exclusion.
Panellists: Izidor Mlakar (AI4HOPE), Alexander Varjord (INSPIRE), Jan Hrdlička (VR Talks)
